chapter: Kansas City, Omaha and Lloyd Hunter
title: Rescued by a farmer who kept them a week
summary: The baritone player found a farmhouse; the farmer took the thirteen of them in by sled, fed them for a week and charged nothing.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: -- baritone player, he put on another overcoat over the coat he had, and he got out. And he started walking and looked like something just cleared the snow, just like that. And then he looked across and he saw a light, way across in the field somewhere. And he couldn't see no more. And he just started walking towards where he thought he saw that light.
And he found this house. And this guy came and got us in one of those sleds.
A black guy or a white guy?
White guy.
For heaven's sake, a human being.
Oh, they were real great out West, really.
Were they?
They certainly were.
Is that so?
Yeah. And they came and got us in this sled.
Honestly?
A wagon with the sled. No wheels, but this man took us to his house and kept us in his house the whole week, all of us, and fed us.
All week?
A whole week, before we could get out.
Oh, I don't believe it.
That's right.
A week before you could get out?

Before we could get out. And when it stopped and we could get into town, he carried us into town in this wagon, sled, to the hotel. And then he wired Omaha for some money, the office, and they sent us some money to pay our hotel bill.
We still didn't play there after we got to the hotel, because of the snow, see. We stayed there three days longer at the hotel.
Gus, you people would have died if you'd been stuck a week in the snow.
That's right, sure, sure. This guy, he came and got us. Anna Mae Winburn was singing with us, at the time.
Well, that's a story, isn't it? Did anybody do anything for that guy?
Yes, we sent him some money. He didn't charge us one penny. But we sent him some money.
Wasn't that a marvelous story?
When we was getting in the --
Well, how could he put up -- how many guys were there, 13?
Thirteen of us altogether.
How could he sleep you?
Well, we just slept on the floor and cuddled up.
Cuddled up, and like that. And the guitar player had blisters the size of a dollar on his hands from frostbite. I just couldn't move my feet, I could just barely move my feet.
By the time you got --
Yeah, when we got to the house.
My gosh.
From the bus to his house, and --
What time of day?
It was late in the evening, see, because we was playing that night, see, --
Yeah. You were nearly there.
Yeah, we were nearly there, see.
Yeah.
And we got stuck, and we just couldn't move.
What do you think happened to those
people in the cars ahead of you?
I don't know. We don't know what happened to them. I really don't know. They got out in time, something like that.
Yeah, yeah.

But this guy, he put us up, fed us and everything. But when he came to pick us up, we were so cold, I was getting in the wagon, the sled, on the sides, and I said, 'Oh, Lord help me,' one of those things like that. And the Lord said, -- I wasn't talking to the Lord. The Lord said, 'Ain't nothing I can do for you.' I said, 'Oh, shut up, I'm not talking to you.' (Laughter.) He said, 'I thought you was talking to me.' I said, 'No.'
Very funny. Was he a funny guy?

Oh, yeah, he was a funny cat. He was a very nice guy. Annamae Winburn had less clothes on that we did, and she didn't get frostbit or anything. And the women can stand the cold, I think, better than men. I'm telling you.
What an experience.
Yeah, that was something else.
Oh, my gosh.
But we --
And so -- but your office sent you money.
Oh, yes.
They didn't leave you in the hole.
Oh, no.
Who was the office, did you know?
I'm going to have to look in this book.
The Kansas City office.
No, no.
Omaha?
Omaha office, the office out of Omaha. That's where the band was from.
Oh, yes, I see. Yeah, fancy that.
So that whole time that band was on the road then, you didn't really play locations.
No.
No.
No locations.
